extracted.intended_audience: students, journalism students, and general readers interested in media hoaxes and document authentication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative criteria for assessing the authenticity of purportedly historical documents (memos) and for appropriate journalistic verification before publication or broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with period-appropriate technology
rubrics_metrics.description: A document's typographical features must be consistent with the technology available at the claimed time (e.g., Times New Roman and Microsoft Word did not exist on typewriters in 1972).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the document's typeface, character shapes, and spacing against what was available in the purported era; the page notes that Times New Roman was not available on 1970s typewriters and that IBM's first PC was introduced in 1981, making modern fonts suspect for 1972-era documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typeface and spacing exact-match test (MS Word comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: If reproducing the document text in modern word-processing defaults (e.g., MS Word Times New Roman, default parameters) yields an exact match in character appearance and spacing, the document is likely a modern forgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows that Word produced an exact reproduction of the CBS memo — identical character shapes and space increments — and argues that this exact match is strong evidence of a computer-produced document. Use reproduced output to check for exact alignment of characters and inter-character spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superscript and special-character diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Small typographical details (such as a superscript 'th') can indicate production method; superscripts produced on a manual typewriter will have characteristic shapes/placements different from computer fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peter Tytell identified the 'th' superscript as a clue; the page notes that a genuine ANG 'th' was produced on an Olympia manual typewriter and that the CBS memos' 'th' was not. Inspect such small details closely as they can rapidly reveal inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with authenticated exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the questioned document to known authentic exemplars prepared on the claimed equipment (e.g., Bush's personnel record typed on an Olympia manual typewriter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page suggests studying a known personnel record prepared on a typewriter to observe format and typographic differences. Use side-by-side comparisons of character shapes, spacing, and layout with authenticated documents from the same source/time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue and analyze contrary expert opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and investigators must solicit, pursue, and analyze expert warnings that cast doubt on a document's authenticity rather than only seeking experts who defend the item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Independent Review Panel criticized CBS for not pursuing Peter Tytell's detailed objections; the page emphasizes that Tytell's views 'were not pursued or analyzed' because the program sought only defending experts. Follow up on contrary expert claims thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heed document examiner warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings from document examiners should be taken seriously and investigated before using documents in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states that document examiners engaged by CBS gave warnings about authenticity which were ignored; treat examiner cautions as substantive leads requiring investigation rather than dismissing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-of-custody and source credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and verify the chain of custody and the credibility of sources who provide documents; undisclosed or dishonest sourcing undermines authenticity claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBS received the memos from Bill Burkett, who initially lied about his source and refused to identify the original provider. Verify how a document was obtained and whether the provider is reliable and transparent about provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a rigorous/scientific method in forensic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a systematic, scientific approach when analyzing typographical or forensic evidence: outline hypotheses, perform controlled reproductions, and document methods and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page points to Dr. Joseph Newcomer's 'scientific' dissection that outlines and uses the scientific method for typographical analysis. Rigorous methodologies and reproducible tests strengthen forensics conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical evidence can supersede content analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical/typographical inconsistencies alone can be sufficient to declare documents inauthentic; content analysis is not always necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page asserts that the memos 'can be shown to be fakes on the basis of typographical evidence alone' and that 'analysis of the content is not necessary.' Therefore, prioritize objective mechanical tests when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confirmation bias in editorial decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reporters must avoid the 'will to believe' that leads them to ignore mounting contrary evidence; actively seek disconfirming data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from the Independent Review Panel: a 'fierce conviction' that the story was true led CBS to ignore evidence. The page labels this behavior as 'Confirmation Bias' and warns journalists that wanting a story to be true can produce grave errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: publish original materials for independent review
rubrics_metrics.description: Making scanned copies (PDFs) or originals available allows outside experts and the public to examine the evidence and can reveal issues missed internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBS posted pdf copies of the scanned memos, enabling bloggers and experts to analyze them; the page implies that public availability aided discovery of the forgery. However, transparency alone is not a substitute for internal verification prior to broadcast.
